A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SMAC method and offline-to-online reinforcement learning study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark experiments, learning curves, regret measurements, connectivity analyses, and ablations, including Figures 6–16 and Tables 1–5.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds experiments on same-objective fine-tuning, compute matching, large-data Door transfer, Hopper-medium, and OGBench Cube.

M1.justification: Section 6 retains the same RvS-conditioned diffusion score estimator, state-dependent scaling network, score-matching critic loss, action-sampling mixture, SAC actor objective, and Muon optimizer. Algorithm 1 is unchanged; the rewritten motivation does not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Appendix L adds Hopper-medium, whose demonstrations exclude extreme failure trajectories, and OGBench Cube, whose preset-motion behavior data can be unrelated or counterproductive to the task. These broaden the evaluated data regimes beyond the retained benchmarks, particularly by testing behavior not generated by an actor-critic policy.

E2.justification: V3 adds IQL-to-IQL and CalQL-to-CalQL as evaluated online comparison methods in Kitchen, alongside SAC fine-tuning (Appendix I, Figures 14–15). The main offline comparator set remains CalQL/CQL, IQL, and TD3+BC. AWR was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: V3 adds controlled evaluation designs: continuing the offline objective during Kitchen fine-tuning, and training IQL for 3 times and CalQL for 2 times as many offline gradient steps to approximately match SMAC's computation (Appendices I and K). These supplement the retained 5,000-example warm start, 50/50 replay mixture, and 200,000-step online evaluation.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether objective mismatch explains instability, whether same-objective endpoints avoid interpolation valleys, and whether extra baseline compute closes the transfer gap. Appendix J also extends the existing large-dataset investigation with a direct SMAC comparison. The batch-size, RvS, score-identity, kappa, and Muon analyses from v1 remain.

E5.justification: Section 4 newly states that offline-to-online pairs use five seeds per environment unless otherwise noted. Figure 4's four-seed specification was already present. This is additional run-count disclosure, not evidence of increased runs; the existing regret uncertainty entries remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Figures 14–18 add findings that same-objective Kitchen fine-tuning avoids the sharp collapse but improves more slowly, extra baseline compute does not close the Kitchen gap, and SMAC transfers stably in the additional settings. Tables 1–5 and the original plotted results are retained, including SMAC's normalized SAC regret of 0.031. These are additional results, not improved scores under the original settings.

T1.justification: The maximum-entropy score-gradient identity, linear-connectivity definition, and formal problem statement are retained. The SAC and PPO derivations remain in Appendix U, formerly Appendix P. Condensed background mathematics and the rewritten geometric motivation introduce no new formal result or transfer guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: a geometric explanation of transfer instability and SMAC as an offline method supporting smooth online adaptation. Both retain smooth SAC/TD3 transfer on six D4RL tasks and the 34–58% regret reduction in four environments. The added experiments support these existing headline claims.

C2.justification: V3 substantially reframes the mechanism as using an offline-estimable score proxy to shape critic geometry, explicitly stating that dataset optimality and exact offline satisfaction of the identity are unnecessary. It adds interpretations of the objective and compute controls, qualifies transfer to arbitrary online algorithms, and expands limitations concerning computational cost and benchmark-dependent connectivity evidence.

D1.justification: V3 discloses roughly 3–4 GPU hours for diffusion training on one L40S, total offline costs relative to IQL and CalQL, and coarse manual selection of kappa. Captions also clarify that the main learning curves omit the first 200,000 offline gradient steps. Existing hyperparameter values and pseudocode are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds Black et al. (2024) on pi0 and removes references including Ajay et al., Janner et al., Juneja et al., Ghosal et al., and Bobu et al. alongside condensed background and motivation. The substantive positioning against the closest offline RL methods in Section 8 remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, method motivation, limitations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 7 is reorganized into five question-based subsections, the experimental setup is consolidated, and AWR receives a dedicated appendix discussion. This substantially changes the narrative independently of the new experiments.

P2.justification: V3 adds five substantive figures, numbered 14–18, while retaining the original sixteen figures. The previous kappa and Muon figures become Figures 19–21. Tables and figures are redistributed throughout the document, including moving Table 1 earlier and separating the appendix regret and hyperparameter tables across different pages; several captions are revised.

improvement.justification: The new same-objective and compute-matched Kitchen controls address alternative explanations left less directly tested in v1, while added coverage and cost/seed disclosures improve credibility and transparency. The gain is limited by sparse protocol and uncertainty documentation for the new experiments. Figure 15 also labels visibly nonmonotone interpolation curves as linearly connected despite the paper's monotonicity definition, weakening that particular interpretation.
